title: French Omelette
subtitle: pale, set on the outside, just custardy within
excerpt: The French omelette is a test of technique. It should be pale yellow, with no colour, rolled or folded rather than flat. The inside stays soft and just set. Three eggs, butter, and seasoning are all you need.
sourceNotes: The French omelette is one of the foundational tests of classical French cooking. Escoffier and later Julia Child both described it as a benchmark dish for young cooks.

content.text: The pan must be hot before the eggs go in. Use a non-stick pan if possible. Work quickly -- the whole process takes about 90 seconds.
Beat the eggs with a fork until the yolks and whites are fully combined. Season with salt and pepper.
Heat a 20cm non-stick pan over high heat until very hot. Add the butter and let it melt and foam.
Pour in the eggs. Immediately shake the pan and stir with a spatula to scramble the eggs slightly. Then let them settle for 15 seconds.
Tilt the pan and use the spatula to fold the near edge of the omelette over the centre. Roll it out onto a plate, seam side down.
It should be pale golden outside and softly set within. Serve at once.

items.cause: Pan too hot or butter burned
items.fix: Reduce heat slightly. The omelette should cook with no colour.
Remove from the heat while the centre still looks slightly wet -- it continues cooking from residual heat.

content.text: The French omelette is a cornerstone of French cuisine and one of the first dishes taught in professional kitchens. It looks simple but demands precise heat and timing. A good omelette is pale, rolled, and soft inside -- a bad one is flat, brown, and rubbery. This is a dish worth practising until it becomes automatic.
